earlier_scan.note: Bookkeeping languoid (retired ISO mly); Marsden: accent on long/penult syllable, default former syllable, weak stress; some final-stress words (besar).

new_statements.quote: With respect to the Malayan it is sufficient to observe, that long syllables, or syllables containing a long vowel, are generally, though not always accented, especially in a final syllable; that when the first syllable of a dissyllable or penultimate of a trisyllable is long, it is always accented, as būnoh to kill, tākut afraid, kapāla the head; that when both syllables are long, the former only has a perceptible accent, as mālū ashamed, mārī come, tūlī deaf; that when both syllables are short, an accent is in general given to the first; or, it may be said, that in all doubtful cases the accent inclines to the former rather than to the latter syllable; as lambat slow, ganti to change, kanal to recollect, but in certain words, as besár great, kechíl little, balúm not yet, a decided stress is laid upon the last.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent goes with vowel 'length' (= plene-written alif/wau/ya in Jawi): a long penult (first syllable of a disyllable, penult of a trisyllable) is always accented; if both syllables are long only the penult is perceptibly accented; if both are short the accent generally still falls on the first/penult ('in all doubtful cases the accent inclines to the former'); a lexical set (besár, kechíl, balúm — all schwa-penult words) has decided final stress. Net effect: penultimate accent, final in schwa-penult words; Marsden adds (same page) that 'the accent or syllabic emphasis in Malayan words is for the most part much less strong than in the languages of Europe', and p.26 that most primitives are disyllables 'pronounced with a slight stress or accent on the former of the two'. On suffixation (pp.118-119) the long vowel of the root penult is shortened and the following syllable lengthened, i.e. accent shifts rightward to the new penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Marsden (Crawfurd 1852 p.cix adds a second accent on the first syllable of polysyllables).
new_statements.exceptions: 'in certain words, as besár great, kechíl little, balúm not yet, a decided stress is laid upon the last' (schwa-penult words); long syllables 'generally, though not always accented, especially in a final syllable'; derivatives with annexed particles shift length/accent to the following syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms of 'primitive' words and their suffixed derivatives, judged largely from Jawi plene spelling); accent explicitly described as weak. Modern instrumental descriptions of the successor languoid Standard Malay (Zuraidah et al. 2008; Clynes & Deterding 2011 p.265) find no lexical stress, only phrase-final rise-fall prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: mala1546 is a Glottolog BOOKKEEPING languoid for the retired ISO 639-3 code [mly] 'Malay (individual language)', split on 2008-02-18 (change request 2007-183) into Standard Malay [zsm] = stan1306, Malay [zlm] = mala1479, Haji [hji] and Papuan Malay [pmy]. It is not a distinct language. The catalog already holds Standard Malay (stan1306) via Winstedt 1913 'Malay Grammar' sec.14, and the sister our files holds the [zlm] sources. The single Glottolog ref attached to mala1546, Marsden 1812, describes the literary/spoken Malay of Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula c.1800 as written in Jawi script (his 'long vowels' are the plene letters alif/wau/ya); it belongs as an older-primary reference under stan1306/mala1479, not as a new catalog entity (a retired code does not make a separate language). His three final-stress 'exceptions' besár, kechíl, balúm are all schwa-penult words, i.e. the same schwa->final rule later stated by Favre 1876 and Winstedt 1913/1945; modern instrumental work (Zuraidah et al. 2008; Clynes & Deterding 2011) finds no lexical stress in Standard Malay.

sources.locator: 'Of Prosody. — Of Quantity.', printed p.118 (archive.org PDF leaf 178); supporting remark under 'Division of Words', printed p.26 (PDF leaf 86)
sources.note: 'Of Prosody / Of Quantity' p.118 (page scan read): long (plene-written) penult of a di-/trisyllable is always accented; both long -> only the former accented; both short -> accent generally on the first, 'in all doubtful cases the accent inclines to the former'; certain words (besár, kechíl, balúm) have decided stress on the last; accent overall much weaker than in European languages. Also p.26: most primitives are dissyllables 'pronounced with a slight stress or accent on the former of the two'.

sources.citation: Clynes, Adrian & David Deterding. 2011. Standard Malay (Brunei). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(2): 259-268. doi:10.1017/S002510031100017X
sources.note: p.265 'Stress and intonation': 'There appears to be no inherent lexical stress in the Standard Malay of Brunei'; phrase-level rise-fall over the penultimate and final syllables of a phrase; variable final vs penult prominence 'consistent with an absence of lexical stress'. (Describes stan1306, successor of [mly].)

sources.citation: Zuraidah Mohd Don, Gerry Knowles & Janet Yong. 2008. How words can be misleading: a study of syllable timing and 'stress' in Malay. The Linguistics Journal 3(2). (Internet Archive copy of the HTML article)
sources.note: Abstract: preliminary word-list study 'seemed to provide strong evidence for penultimate stress.. the evidence collapsed.. Malay does not have word stress at all'; Conclusion: 'there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonologists call stress'. (Peninsular Standard Malay = stan1306.)

sources.citation: Winstedt, Richard O. [1945]. Colloquial Malay: a grammar with conversations. New edition revised. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner. (DLI scan, archive.org dli.ernet.78799)
sources.note: 'Accent' p.4: 'There is no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word. Ordinarily the stress, such as it is, falls on the penultimate.. the only important exception being that when the penultimate is ĕ in an open syllable and rarely in a closed, then the stress falls on the last syllable'; suffixed words keep root stress with prolonged new penult.

sources.citation: Winstedt, R.O. 1913. Malay Grammar. Oxford: Clarendon Press. sec.14 'Accent' pp.30-32 (archive.org malaygrammar00winsrich)
sources.note: Already the catalog's the deciding source for Standard Malay: no strong accent; ordinarily penult; final when penult is open schwa; prefixal derivatives of monosyllabic roots and vocatives sometimes final.

sources.citation: Favre, P. 1876. Grammaire de la langue malaise. Vienne: Imprimerie imperiale et royale. (archive.org grammairedelalan00favr)
sources.note: sec.36 'De l'accent' pp.34-35: accent very weak (realised as lengthening); general but not absolute tendency to the penult; Rule 1 penult open-long or closed -> penult; Rule 2 penult open and short (schwa) -> final (berí, serú, belúm, benár); suffixed derivatives take penult of the whole or keep the root accent.

sources.citation: Crawfurd, John. 1852. A Grammar and Dictionary of the Malay Language, vol. 1 (Dissertation and Grammar). London: Smith, Elder. (archive.org grammardictionar00craw)
sources.note: Preliminary Dissertation p.cix: 'Accent, in the Malay.. is a very simple and easy matter. In bisyllabic and trisyllabic words, it is, with very few exceptions, on the penultimate, and in polysyllabic words, without exception, there are two accents, one on the first and one on the penultimate syllable.'
